verdict.rationale: The word-pattern across the cited passages lines the Spirit's presence up with order and tested speech rather than with unbounded ecstatic display. In 1 Corinthians 14:33 God is described negatively as not a God of disorder or tumult (akatastasias, Strong's G0181, attested 5 times across 1 Corinthians 14:33, 2 Corinthians 6:5, 2 Corinthians 12:20, James 3:16, Luke 21:9, always with a negative sense) and positively as the God of peace (eirenes, Strong's G1515, 92 New Testament occurrences, spread across the whole Bible). The same chapter at 14:40 commands that all things be done decently (euschemonos, Strong's G2156, 3 occurrences across 1 Corinthians 14:40, Romans 13:13, 1 Thessalonians 4:12, every New Testament use governing visible bodily conduct) and according to arranged order (kata taxin, from taxis Strong's G5010). The immediate regulation in 1 Corinthians 14:27-32 makes the same pattern explicit lexically: an interpreter is required (diermeneutes, Strong's G1329), others judge or evaluate prophecy (diakrino, Strong's G1252, in 14:29), and the spirits of the prophets are SUBJECT to the prophets (hypotasso, Strong's G5293, in 14:32). Deuteronomy 18:20-22 supplies a verification test rather than a description of intensity, judging a self-asserted prophetic word by whether it actually happens and exposing proud or insolent speech (the verb to act presumptuously, zid, Strong's H2102, and its cognate noun presumption, zadon, Strong's H2087). 1 John 4:1 commands test the spirits (dokimazete ta pneumata, from dokimazo Strong's G1381) precisely because many false prophets (pseudoprophetai, Strong's G5578) have gone out, and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 anchors the same verb test (dokimazo) applied to prophetic utterance. Treating ecstatic phenomena as the standard measure of the Spirit therefore runs against the dense, whole-Bible pattern of tested, orderly, fulfillment-checked speech.

scripture.reasoning: God is described negatively, against disorder or tumult or confusion (akatastasia, with 5 New Testament occurrences all carrying a negative sense), and positively as the God of peace (eirene, with 92 New Testament occurrences, spread across the whole Bible in Pauline, Johannine and Petrine usage). The grammatical phrase 'not of disorder is God but of peace' (a 'from-X' grammatical form called a genitive of quality, ou estin akatastasias ho theos alla eirenes) ties God's own character to peaceful order, making disorder in the assembly inconsistent with the Spirit as the source.

The closing command 'let all things be done decently and according to order' (panta de euschemonos kai kata taxin ginestho) directs that everything in corporate worship happen decently and according to arranged order. The adverb decently (euschemonos, 3 New Testament occurrences, every instance governing visible bodily conduct: Romans 13:13 walking properly, 1 Thessalonians 4:12 walking properly toward outsiders, 1 Corinthians 14:40 corporate gifts) and the phrase according to order (kata taxin) set a governing norm of seemly behavior and arrangement over how the gifts described in the surrounding chapter are exercised. The third-person command 'let it be done' (ginestho) expresses a standing rule, not a one-time request.

The ongoing command 'test the spirits whether they are from God' (dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou theou estin) is grounded by 'because many false prophets have gone out into the world' (hoti polloi pseudoprophetai exelelythasin eis ton kosmon). The same verb test (dokimazo) appears at 1 Thessalonians 5:21 commanding 'test all things' (dokimazete panta) over prophetic utterance specifically, anchoring the test-the-spirits command as a norm shared by Paul and John. Spiritual claims are put under evaluation rather than accepted simply because of how they appeared, because false prophets are present in the world, so dramatic display does not by itself prove the Spirit.

The prophet who proudly or insolently speaks (yazid, the Hebrew causative form 'to cause to do' of the verb to act presumptuously, zid, attested 10 times with a consistent meaning of proud or insolent self-assertion in Deuteronomy 1:43, Deuteronomy 17:13, Deuteronomy 18:20, Nehemiah 9:10, Nehemiah 9:16, Nehemiah 9:29, Jeremiah 50:29) a word in the LORD's name that was not commanded, or who speaks in the name of other gods, is to die. The criterion fixes attention on the source and authorization of the word, not on its intensity or any ecstatic accompaniment.

The observable test is whether the spoken word (davar) comes to pass and is fulfilled. A word that does not happen marks speech spoken in presumption (bezadon, from the cognate noun of zid, attested 11 times across Deuteronomy, Samuel, Proverbs, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Obadiah with the same arrogance meaning). The people are not to fear it. The standard is verification by fulfillment, an outside check that bypasses subjective experience entirely.

complicating_texts.resolution: The same chapter that commands order also says 'do not forbid speaking in tongues' (me koluete lalein glossais), so the orderly-worship norm in 1 Corinthians 14:40 does not suppress the gifts but governs how they are exercised. The proposition targets treating ecstatic phenomena as the standard measure, not the existence of the gifts, so 1 Corinthians 14:39 is consistent with the verdict.

Pentecost onlookers mocked the disciples as filled with new wine (sweet new wine, gleukos, Strong's G1098), which could suggest a disorderly appearance. The narrative resolves it by its own word-choices: Acts 2:6 reports each one heard them speaking in their own native language (dialektos, Strong's G1258, an intelligible native language), and Peter then delivers a structured doctrinal address in Acts 2:14-36. The episode therefore shows understandable, content-bearing speech, not ecstatic spectacle, as the proof of the Spirit. The mockery records an outsider misreading, not the actual word-pattern of the event.

Paul caps tongues at two or three (two, dyo Strong's G1417; three, treis Strong's G5140), 'in turn' (meros, Strong's G3313 'part' and ana, Strong's G0303 'each'), with an interpreter required (diermeneutes, Strong's G1329), and requires silence if none is present. The numerical and procedural limits encoded in these explicit words confirm that even genuine gift-exercise is bounded and orderly, reinforcing rather than complicating the verdict that uncontrolled phenomena are not the norm.

The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets (pneumata propheton prophetais hypotassetai, with subject hypotasso Strong's G5293, the verb here in the ongoing passive form, an ongoing, simple statement of being-subjected). The lexical claim is direct: prophetic spiritual experience is voluntarily controllable by the prophet, not an overriding force. This shuts out the reading that loss-of-control phenomena are the Spirit's standard signature.

'Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge' (Prophetai de dyo e treis laleitosan, kai hoi alloi diakrinetosan, with judge diakrino Strong's G1252, others judge or evaluate). The very class of utterance most associated with ecstatic immediacy is put under community evaluation, parallel to the verb test (dokimazo) in 1 John 4:1 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21. This reinforces the verdict.

variants.note: The cited verses lie outside the 3 John CBGM sample scope (the New Testament textual variants tracked in the editorial sample). The known variant at 1 Corinthians 14:40 concerns the position of the connector 'and' or 'but' (de), which does not touch the 'decently and according to order' (euschemonos kai kata taxin) clause that carries the verdict, so no variant materially affects the reading. The question about whether 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 is an insertion does not bear on the cited verses.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reading that views the miraculous sign-gifts as concluded still affirms the proposition on the same word-based ground, since the order, peace, and testing vocabulary (disorder or akatastasia, peace or eirene, decently or euschemonos, order or taxis, test or dokimazo, judge or diakrino, be subject or hypotasso) describes how the Spirit operates in any era and rules out ecstatic spectacle as the diagnostic of His presence.

A reading that holds the gifts to continue also affirms the proposition in its strongest form: the very chapter that permits tongues ('do not forbid' or me koluete in 1 Corinthians 14:39) and prophecy is the same chapter that places them under 'decently and according to order' (euschemonos kai kata taxin, 1 Corinthians 14:40), under testing by the verbs test (dokimazo) and judge (diakrino) in 1 John 4:1 and 1 Corinthians 14:29, and under being subject (hypotasso) in 1 Corinthians 14:32 (prophets' spirits subject to prophets). Continued operation is therefore consistent with, and in fact requires, orderly and tested exercise. Hyper-charismatic excess as defined here (uncontrolled tongues, false prophecies, manipulative miracles) is what these very texts regulate against.

A position that holds judgment on whether the sign-gifts have ceased but applies the New Testament regulation strictly still affirms, because the regulation itself is what the proposition asserts. The lay-summary nuance applies: the texts fix the principle (order and testing) decisively but leave the precise contextual boundary between Spirit-led contribution and disorder to be worked out by the gathered, judging community (1 Corinthians 14:29).

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses converge because the verdict turns on the order, peace, and testing word-fields, not on whether sign-gifts persist. The proposition concerns the standard measure of the Spirit's presence, which the lexical data locates in tested, orderly, fulfillment-verified speech rather than in dramatic phenomena. The remaining underdetermination in the words is scope, not direction: the texts forbid disorder but do not enumerate every contested borderline practice.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does the New Testament establish orderly and tested worship as the standard for recognizing the Spirit's presence, or does it present dramatic ecstatic phenomena (falling, sustained laughter, conscience-binding prophetic decrees) as the standard evidence?
stem_audit.notes: The phrase 'departs from the New Testament pattern of orderly worship' presupposes both that an orderly pattern is the standard and that ecstatic-centric practice deviates from it, which bundles the conclusion into the stem. The neutralized form poses the question without prejudging which criterion the text endorses. VERDICT-CHANGED: no, the verdict was still derived on the original stem from the lexical data, which independently supports the order, peace, and testing pattern via disorder (akatastasia) versus peace (eirene), 'decently and according to order' (euschemonos kai kata taxin), being-subject (hypotasso) of prophetic spirits, judging (diakrino) by others, testing (dokimazo) at 1 John 4:1 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21, and the Deuteronomic verb to act presumptuously (zid) and noun presumption (zadon) plus the fulfillment test.

lay_summary: The words in these passages point one direction. In 1 Corinthians 14:33 Paul says God is not a God of disorder (akatastasia) but of peace (eirene). Every other New Testament use of disorder (akatastasia) is negative (riots, instability, factional confusion), so the contrast is sharp. The chapter closes in 14:40 with a plain command that everything be done decently (euschemonos, used elsewhere only of walking properly toward outsiders) and in order (kata taxin). Just before that, 14:27 caps tongues at two or three, one at a time, with someone to interpret, and tells the speaker to stay silent if no interpreter is present. 14:29 says when prophets speak the others are to judge (diakrino) what is said. 14:32 says directly that the spirits of prophets are subject (hypotasso) to prophets. Loss-of-control is not the Spirit's signature in this text. In 1 John 4:1 the readers are told to test (dokimazo) the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world, and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 uses the same verb of prophetic utterance specifically. A powerful display is not by itself proof that the Spirit is at work. The word has to be examined. Deuteronomy 18:20-22 adds the same logic from the older covenant. A prophet who speaks presumptuously (from the verb zid and noun zadon, words that carry arrogant self-assertion across Deuteronomy, Samuel, Proverbs, Jeremiah) a word that was never commanded is condemned, and the test of a true word is whether it actually comes to pass. The check is fulfillment and authorization, not the intensity of the experience. Reading these texts together, the consistent measure of genuine spiritual speech is that it is orderly, intelligible, subject to testing, and verified by fulfillment. Making dramatic ecstatic phenomena such as falling, sustained laughter, or binding prophetic decrees the standard evidence of the Spirit does not match this pattern. Where readers differ is not the principle but the exact boundary case. The vocabulary fixes that the Spirit operates in order and submits to testing, but it does not enumerate every contested practice, so the gathered community has to judge particulars (14:29 again). Both a view that the sign-gifts have ceased and a view that they continue land in the same place here, because the order, peace, and testing language describes how the Spirit works regardless of which gifts remain in operation.
